lessons.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) on a Budget
lessons.body: You don't need expensive gear to stay safe. Start with a long-sleeved shirt and trousers made of thick cotton, not nylon. Nylon melts if it catches fire and doesn't absorb sweat. Wear a wide-brimmed hat or a scarf wrapped around your head and neck. For your face, use a simple dust mask (N95 if you can get it) or a double layer of cloth. For eyes, wear tight-fitting sunglasses or clear safety glasses from a hardware shop. For hands, use rubber gloves â the thick ones for washing dishes work. For feet, wear rubber boots, not sandals. If you can't afford boots, wear closed shoes and tuck your trousers into socks. Always wash your PPE separately from family clothes after each use. Store PPE in a clean plastic bag or bucket away from pesticides. Never wear PPE inside the house. Check for tears or holes before each use. Replace gloves when they get sticky or cracked. A cheap raincoat can serve as an apron when mixing. Remember: pesticides enter through skin, lungs, and eyes. Cover all three. If you feel dizzy, stop, wash, and get fresh air. Don't reuse disposable masks more than once. In hot weather, take breaks to avoid heat stress. A simple kit costs less than 5000 shillings (about $40) and lasts a season.

lessons.title: Mixing and Loading Pesticides Safely
lessons.body: Always mix pesticides outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed, never in the kitchen or near food. Read the label twice: it tells you the correct dose, like 30 ml per 15 liters of water. Use a dedicated measuring jug and stirring stick â never use them for food afterwards. Wear your PPE: gloves, mask, glasses, long sleeves. Pour water into the sprayer tank first, then add the pesticide. This reduces splashing. Never mix more than you need for one day. If you must mix concentrates, do it on a concrete or plastic sheet so spills can be contained. If you spill, cover with sand or sawdust, sweep it up, and bury it away from water sources. Wash your hands and face immediately after mixing, even if you wore gloves. Never eat, drink, or smoke while mixing. Keep children and animals away. Store pesticides in their original labelled containers, locked in a cupboard. Never transfer to a soda bottle â someone might drink it. After loading, close the tank tightly and rinse the outside with water. Pour rinse water into the sprayer, not on the ground. For wettable powders, make a paste first in a small bucket, then add to the tank. Always triple-rinse empty containers before disposal. If you feel sick, call for help and show the label to the health worker.

lessons.title: Calibrating a Knapsack Sprayer
lessons.body: Calibration means finding out how much liquid your sprayer puts out per hectare, so you apply the right dose. First, mark a test area of 100 square meters (10 m by 10 m). Fill your sprayer with clean water to a known level, like 10 liters. Pump to the pressure you will use in the field (usually 2-3 bars). Walk at your normal spraying pace across the 100 mÂ², keeping the nozzle at the same height (about 50 cm above the crop). After spraying, measure how much water you used. For example, if you used 2 liters, then you use 2 liters per 100 mÂ². Since 1 hectare = 10,000 mÂ², multiply by 100: you use 200 liters per hectare. Now check the label: if it says apply 1 liter of pesticide per hectare, you need to add 1 liter to 200 liters of water. But if your sprayer only holds 15 liters, you add 1/13 of that dose (about 75 ml) to a full tank. Repeat calibration for each crop and growth stage. Nozzle wear increases flow â replace worn nozzles. Always calibrate with water, not pesticide. Keep a record of your calibration. If you change walking speed or pressure, recalibrate. A simple calibration test takes 15 minutes and saves money and protects your crop.

lessons.title: Best Times to Spray: Weather and Pest Activity
lessons.body: Spray when the wind is calm â below 10 km/h. Early morning (6-9 am) and late afternoon (4-6 pm) are best. Avoid midday heat because spray evaporates or burns leaves. Also avoid spraying when rain is expected within 6 hours; rain washes pesticide off. Check the weather: if leaves are wet from dew, wait until they dry. For pests, target when they are active. Many caterpillars feed at night, so evening spraying works. Aphids and whiteflies are active in the morning. Fungal diseases spread in cool, humid conditions, so spray preventively before symptoms. Don't spray when bees are foraging â early morning or evening when flowers are closed. Never spray on windy days; drift can damage nearby crops and harm people. Use a calm-day test: light a candle or watch smoke; if smoke goes sideways, it's too windy. Temperature matters: above 30Â°C, pesticides can volatilize and drift. Also, high humidity can cause droplets to stay wet longer, increasing absorption â good for systemic pesticides but risky for you. Wear PPE even in heat. If you must spray in hot weather, take breaks in shade. Always monitor the forecast. A simple rule: if you can't see the spray cloud settle, it's too windy. Spray when pests are young and before they multiply.

lessons.title: Avoiding Drift and Contamination of Water Sources
lessons.body: Drift is when spray moves off-target. To avoid it, spray when wind is below 10 km/h and use a coarse nozzle (like a flat fan or hollow cone) at low pressure. Keep the nozzle close to the crop â no more than 50 cm above the canopy. Don't spray near water bodies: keep at least 30 meters away from rivers, streams, wells, and lakes. Never fill your sprayer directly from a water source; use a bucket and fill downstream. Mix and rinse at least 50 meters from any water. If you spill, contain it with soil and do not wash it into drains. For wells, ensure a concrete apron and a lid. Use buffer zones: plant tall crops like maize or hedges between fields and water. If you must spray near water, use a shielded sprayer or hand-held wiper. Never clean your sprayer in a river. Instead, rinse in a designated area on your farm, away from wells. Triple-rinse containers and pour rinse water into the sprayer tank for the next load. Do not dump leftover spray on the ground; apply it to a labeled area. Remember: pesticides can seep into groundwater and poison drinking water for years. Protect your family and community. Always store pesticides away from water sources. If you see dead fish or sick animals after spraying, report to authorities.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Disposing of Empty Containers
lessons.body: After spraying, clean your equipment immediately. Wear gloves and PPE. Triple-rinse the sprayer tank: fill with clean water, shake, and spray the rinse water onto a labeled crop area â not near water. Do the same for the outside of the tank. Never leave pesticide in the tank overnight. For empty containers, triple-rinse them as well: fill each container one-third with water, cap, shake for 30 seconds, and pour the rinse water into the sprayer tank for the next application. Repeat two more times. Then puncture or crush the container so it cannot be reused for food or water. Never burn containers â burning releases toxic fumes. Never reuse containers for drinking water, food, or household items. The best disposal is to take them to a licensed hazardous waste facility. If none exists, bury them deep (at least 50 cm) away from water sources, or return to the supplier if they have a take-back program. Some agro-dealers collect empty containers. Do not throw them in the bush or river. Store rinsed containers in a secure place until disposal. Wash your hands and clothes after handling. Remember: a rinsed container still has traces of poison. Keep children away. Follow local regulations. If you are unsure, ask your extension officer. Proper disposal protects your family, livestock, and the environment.

quiz.q: What type of clothing is recommended for spraying pesticides?
options: B) Thick cotton long-sleeved shirt and trousers
quiz.explanation: Cotton absorbs sweat and does not melt like nylon, providing better protection.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix pesticides in the kitchen?
options: B) It may contaminate food and utensils
quiz.explanation: Pesticides can splash onto food and surfaces, causing poisoning.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calibrating a knapsack sprayer?
options: B) Mark a test area of 100 mÂ²
quiz.explanation: A known test area allows you to measure output per unit area.

quiz.q: When is the best time to spray to avoid drift?
options: B) When wind is below 10 km/h
quiz.explanation: Calm conditions reduce spray drift off-target.

quiz.q: How far should you stay away from water sources when spraying?
quiz.explanation: A 30-meter buffer zone helps prevent contamination of water.

quiz.q: What should you do with empty pesticide containers?
quiz.explanation: Triple-rinsing removes residues, and puncturing prevents reuse.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential for eye protection?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses provide a seal against splashes and aerosols.

quiz.q: What should you do if you spill pesticide concentrate?
options: A) Wash it into a drain
B) Cover with sand and sweep up
quiz.explanation: Absorbing the spill prevents it from spreading or contaminating water.

quiz.q: How do you calculate the spray volume per hectare after calibration?
quiz.explanation: Since 1 hectare = 10,000 mÂ², and you tested 100 mÂ², multiply by 100.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spraying when bees are foraging?
options: B) Bees can be killed, affecting pollination
quiz.explanation: Bees are essential pollinators and are highly sensitive to pesticides.

quiz.q: What is a sign that it is too windy to spray?
quiz.explanation: Sideways smoke indicates wind that can cause drift.

quiz.q: What should you do with rinse water from cleaning sprayer?
options: B) Spray onto labeled crop area
quiz.explanation: Rinse water contains pesticide and should be applied to a crop, not dumped.

quiz.q: How many times should you rinse an empty pesticide container?
quiz.explanation: Triple rinsing is the standard to remove most residues.

quiz.q: What is the recommended nozzle height above the crop?
quiz.explanation: 50 cm is close enough to reduce drift but high enough to cover the target.

quiz.q: Why should you not burn empty pesticide containers?
quiz.explanation: Burning can release harmful chemicals into the air.

quiz.q: What should you wear on your feet when spraying?
quiz.explanation: Rubber boots protect feet from spills and splashes.

quiz.q: What is the correct order when mixing pesticides?
quiz.explanation: Adding pesticide to water reduces splashing and improves mixing.

quiz.q: How often should you calibrate your sprayer?
options: B) Every time you change crop or nozzle
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures correct dose; changes in equipment or conditions require recalibration.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while spraying?
options: B) Stop, wash, and get fresh air
D) Lie down in the field
quiz.explanation: Dizziness may indicate pesticide poisoning; stop and seek fresh air.

quiz.q: Why should you never reuse pesticide containers for food?
options: B) They may contain toxic residues
quiz.explanation: Even after rinsing, traces of pesticide can remain and cause poisoning.

quiz.q: What is a buffer zone?
options: A) An area where you store pesticides
B) A strip of land between sprayed area and water
quiz.explanation: Buffer zones protect water sources from drift and runoff.

quiz.q: Which pest is best controlled by evening spraying?
quiz.explanation: Many caterpillars feed at night, so evening spraying is more effective.

quiz.q: What should you do with leftover spray mix?
options: B) Apply to labeled crop area
quiz.explanation: Leftover mix should be used according to label, not dumped.

quiz.q: How can you test wind direction?
options: B) Watch smoke or use a ribbon
quiz.explanation: Smoke or a ribbon shows wind direction and strength.

quiz.q: What is the minimum distance from a well when mixing pesticides?
quiz.explanation: 50 meters prevents contamination of well water.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a mask when spraying?
options: B) To avoid inhaling pesticide droplets
quiz.explanation: Masks filter out harmful particles and vapors.

quiz.q: What should you do with PPE after spraying?
options: B) Wash separately from family clothes
quiz.explanation: Washing separately prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is the best way to dispose of rinsed containers if no facility exists?
options: B) Bury deep away from water
quiz.explanation: Deep burial prevents leaching and accidental reuse.

quiz.q: Why is calibration important?
options: B) To apply the correct dose
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures you apply the right amount, avoiding under- or over-dosing.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get pesticide on your skin?
options: B) Wash with soap and water
quiz.explanation: Immediate washing with soap and water removes the chemical.
